titel: Adjustable or fixed: rate risk and stress test
kurz: What risk lies in an adjustable-rate mortgage after its initial fixed period, what the rate caps allow in the worst case and how a household can test its financing before signing.

bloecke.md:
A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fixes the rate for the whole term. Anyone who chooses it knows their principal and interest payment to the cent until the loan is repaid. An **adjustable-rate mortgage** (ARM) fixes the rate only for an initial period, typically five, seven or ten years. After that, the rate follows an index, today usually the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), plus a fixed margin, and is reset at regular intervals. This uncertainty is [[Interest rate risk|interest rate risk]], and with an ARM the borrower carries it.

In the base case of this lesson, the purchase price is $500,000, the down payment $100,000 and the loan $400,000. A 30-year fixed-rate loan is assumed at 6.25%, which results in a payment of $2,462.87. The alternative is a 5/6 ARM: the rate is fixed for five years at an assumed 5.75%, then it adjusts every six months. Its payment starts at $2,334.29, $128.58 a month less. Both rates are assumptions for illustration. The ARM has the caps that are common for such loans, written 2/1/5: the rate can rise by at most 2 percentage points at the first adjustment, by at most 1 point at each later adjustment and by at most 5 points over the life of the loan. Gross household income is $150,000 a year, or $12,500 a month, and take-home pay is $8,500 a month.

bloecke.md:
## What the initial saving buys

In the first five years, the ARM saves $128.58 a month, a total of $7,715 in payments. Because the lower rate also repays slightly faster, the balance after five years is $371,049 instead of $373,349 with the fixed-rate loan. The saving is therefore real, but small.

The risk is large in comparison. If the index rises, the payment can increase by 20% at the first reset, from $2,334 to $2,803, and after a year and a half of further increases it reaches $3,552 at the lifetime cap of 10.75%. That is 52% more than at the start and $1,089 a month more than the fixed-rate loan would have cost. The caps limit the rise, but they do not prevent it. They tell you exactly how bad the worst case can get, and that makes the worst case calculable before signing.

bloecke.titel: The lifetime cap as the yardstick
bloecke.md: Affordability of an ARM is decided by the payment at the lifetime cap, not by the start rate. The start rate plus the lifetime cap is the only figure in the loan contract that sets an upper limit for the payment for decades. If the household cannot carry this payment, the ARM is a bet on interest rates.

bloecke.md:
## What the lender checks and what you should check

Lenders must make a reasonable, good-faith determination that the borrower can repay the loan, considering income, assets, employment, existing debts and either the debt-to-income ratio or residual income (12 CFR 1026.43, the ability-to-repay rule). For an ARM, the general rule requires the payment to be calculated at the fully indexed rate or the start rate, whichever is higher, not at an introductory teaser rate. The **debt-to-income ratio** (DTI) divides monthly debt payments by gross monthly income. In the base case, principal, interest, property tax and insurance for the fixed-rate loan come to $3,080, or 24.6% of gross income.

For your own decision, the [[Housing cost ratio|housing cost ratio]] is more suitable, because it uses take-home pay and includes maintenance. It divides the payment plus running costs by take-home pay. In the base case, the running costs are $417 for property tax at 1% of the price, $200 for insurance and $417 for maintenance at 1% of the price, together $1,033 a month. With the fixed-rate loan, that gives $3,496, or 41.1% of $8,500; with the ARM, it starts at 39.6%. The burden is therefore already high before a rate increase or a loss of income comes on top.

bloecke.md: A calculation with today's income overstates the burden, because nominal incomes have usually risen after five years. A calculation with extrapolated income understates it, because the payment at the cap is fixed by contract, whereas income growth is not fixed anywhere. Parental leave, part-time work, a downturn in your industry or illness can make your own income deviate from the development of the economy as a whole, which it only follows on average. You should therefore calculate both variants and decide on the basis of the less favourable result.

A stress test that only changes the interest rate is incomplete. A rate increase affects only ARM borrowers, and only after the initial period. The other scenarios affect income and can hit any borrower at any time, including one with a fixed rate.

bloecke.md:
## Unemployment

Unemployment insurance is run by the states within a federal framework. Benefits replace a portion of prior wages up to a weekly maximum that each state sets and that differs considerably between states; in most states, benefits last up to 26 weeks, in some fewer. For higher earners, the maximum often means that benefits cover well under half of the previous take-home pay.

In the base case, earner A brings home $5,100 and earner B $3,400. If A becomes unemployed and receives an assumed $2,000 a month in benefits, household income falls to $5,400. The housing cost ratio with the fixed-rate loan then rises from 41% to 65%. With a reserve, this can be sustained for several months; without one, it cannot.

There is no general federal program that takes over mortgage payments. What exists is a procedure. A servicer generally may not start a foreclosure before the loan is more than 120 days delinquent (12 CFR 1024.41(f)), and borrowers who apply for help in time are entitled to an evaluation for loss mitigation options such as forbearance, a repayment plan or a loan modification. Forbearance only postpones payments, however; the missed amounts have to be repaid or added to the loan later. Contacting the servicer early keeps more options open than waiting.

## Separation

Legally, separation is the most complicated case, because the deed, the loan and the agreement between the partners diverge. Borrowers who signed the promissory note together are each liable for the full amount. The lender can demand the full payment from either of them, regardless of who moves out and what the divorce decree says, because the decree binds only the spouses. Signing a quitclaim deed removes a partner from the title, but not from the loan.

A release from liability usually requires a refinance in the name of the remaining partner, who must then qualify alone. With a payment of $2,463 plus $617 for tax and insurance on take-home pay of $5,100, that is difficult. A transfer to a spouse as part of a divorce does not allow the lender to call the loan due (Garn-St Germain Act, 12 U.S.C. § 1701j-3), and FHA and VA loans can be assumed with the lender's approval, possibly with a release of the departing borrower. If the co-owners cannot agree, a court can order a partition under state law, which typically ends in a sale below what a private sale would achieve.

bloecke.titel: Why the escape route from an ARM can close
bloecke.md:
Many ARM borrowers plan to sell or refinance before the first reset. Because most loans can be repaid without a penalty, this works as long as four conditions hold at the right time: rates are not much higher than at the start, the house is worth more than the loan, income is stable and the credit history is clean. In 2007 to 2009, these conditions failed together for many borrowers. Prices fell, lenders tightened their standards, and many ARM borrowers could neither sell nor refinance before their payments rose.

A plan to refinance is therefore an option, not a certainty. A household that chooses an ARM should be able to carry the payment at the lifetime cap even without it.

## Affordable financing and rules of thumb

A widespread rule says that housing costs (principal, interest, taxes and insurance) should not exceed 28% of gross income, and all debt payments together not 36%. Lenders' own limits are often higher. The rule has no sound derivation and two systematic flaws.

First, it scales incorrectly. Of $5,000 gross a month, $3,600 remains for taxes and all other expenses after 28% for housing; of $20,000 gross, $14,400 remains. But the second household does not need four times as much to live on. Percentage rules are therefore too generous for low incomes and too strict for high ones.

Second, the result depends entirely on the interest rate level, although the rule does not take it into account. Over 30 years, a payment of $2,400 for principal and interest supports a loan of around $569,000 at 3.0%, a level close to the record lows of 2020 and 2021, but only around $390,000 at 6.25%. The purchasing power of the same household has thus fallen by about a third, without anything having changed in its situation.

Only the residual income calculation is useful. It deducts the measured expenses from take-home pay and determines the affordable payment from what is left, instead of applying a flat percentage. The VA uses a version of this method when it approves loans.

bloecke.md: A reserve of six to twelve monthly payments costs return. However, it is the only protection against a loss of income leading to a forced sale. These costs can be quantified. Anyone who uses the money for extra principal payments instead earns a risk-free return equal to the mortgage rate, here 6.25%, and for households that do not itemize, this return is effectively tax-free. Interest in a high-yield savings account or money market fund is taxed as ordinary income. At a 22% federal tax rate, the account would have to pay 8.01% to draw level, and with an additional 5% state income tax 8.56%. Interest on Treasury bills is exempt from state income tax, which narrows the gap slightly. Nevertheless, the reserve should not go into extra principal payments. Its purpose is to avoid a sale at the wrong time, and for that the return plays no role.

## The fixed rate as an option

In the base case, the fixed rate costs 0.5 percentage points more than the ARM's start rate. Over the first five years, that is $7,715 in higher payments and about $10,000 in additional interest. This is offset by a one-sided right. If rates fall, the fixed-rate borrower can refinance without a penalty and only pays new closing costs. If rates rise, the old rate continues to apply for the full 30 years. The premium is the price of this option.

Whether the option is worthwhile is shown by comparing it with the potential damage. If the ARM's rate stays at 5.75% after the reset, the ARM saves around $46,000 in interest over the full term. If it is reset to 7.75% and stays there, the ARM costs around $94,000 more in interest than the fixed-rate loan. At the lifetime cap, it costs around $310,000 more. Measured against a premium of about $10,000 over five years, that is a ratio that is open to debate, but that should feed into the decision.

mitnehmen: A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage removes interest rate risk for the borrower; with an ARM, the borrower carries it from the end of the initial period.
The payment at the lifetime cap is the yardstick for an ARM: in the example, it is 52% above the start payment and $1,089 a month above the fixed-rate payment.
A stress test calculates with both stagnating and growing income, because the payment at the cap is fixed by contract, but income growth is not.

Unemployment insurance replaces only part of prior wages up to a state maximum, usually for up to 26 weeks; there is no general program that takes over mortgage payments, only the servicer's loss mitigation procedure.
Borrowers who signed the note together each remain liable for the full amount after a separation, whatever the divorce decree says.

begriffe.text: Mortgage with a rate that is fixed for an initial period and then adjusts at regular intervals to an index plus a margin. A 5/6 ARM is fixed for five years and then adjusts every six months.
Limits on how much an ARM's rate can change, usually written as three numbers such as 2/1/5: the maximum change at the first adjustment, at each later adjustment and over the life of the loan.
The two parts of an ARM's rate after the initial period. The index is a market rate such as SOFR and moves; the margin is a fixed markup set in the loan contract.
Monthly debt payments, including the mortgage payment with tax and insurance, divided by gross monthly income. Lenders use it to assess the ability to repay; it ignores taxes and actual living costs.

Payment plus running costs (property tax, insurance, maintenance, HOA dues) in relation to take-home pay. It is more meaningful than the DTI for your own decision, because it includes maintenance and is based on the money actually available.
